titulo: The North Wind and the Sun
caption: YouTube only (a medio in 16:9, no Short and no Reel). What goes out is the YouTube title and the description.
descripcion:
Two forces hold a contest on a road: whoever gets a traveler to take off his cloak wins. The Wind blows with all his might and the traveler holds on tighter. The Sun just shines, and it takes the whole afternoon.

A story for tonight, from a fable credited to Aesop, told again. The fable gives the Wind, the Sun, the traveler, the contest, the harder the blasts the tighter the cloak, and the cloak coming off in the warmth. The scoreboard of gusts, the small amber visitor who asks the Sun how long it will take, the answer the afternoon, the hour-by-hour afternoon and the reading of what each one paid are invented for this retelling, and the video says so. Townsend's version goes on a little past the cloak; this one stops there, and says so.

Sources
Aesop, The North Wind and the Sun, in George Fyler Townsend's English translation (Three Hundred Aesop's Fables), public domain, Project Gutenberg #21: the North Wind and the Sun dispute which is more powerful and agree that the victor will be the one who first strips a wayfaring man of his clothes; the Wind blows with all his might, but the keener his blasts, the closer the traveler wraps his cloak around him; the Sun then shines out with all his warmth and the traveler takes off one garment after another. Townsend's moral is that persuasion beats force. Aesop is a figure of Greek tradition, said to have lived in the sixth century BCE; the fables credited to him were collected and written down by others, and the exact wording changes from edition to edition.

alt: A video in 16:9, a story for tonight. On a country road in daylight, a teal doorway-shaped figure, the traveler, wears a red cloak. On the left a grey cloud, the North Wind, blows streaks of air at him; on the upper right a yellow Sun glows. A card gives the source: Aesop, a Greek storyteller, in the Townsend translation. A sheet shows the Wind's turn, gust one, two and three, each marked tighter, as the traveler holds his cloak closed. The Wind gives up and the Sun starts to shine. In the invented part, Cella, a small amber figure with two white eyes, sits by the road and asks the Sun how long it will take; the Sun says the afternoon. A small clock on the ground runs from noon to four while the cloak loosens. At four o'clock the traveler takes off the cloak and folds it. A sheet shows what each one paid: the Wind a minute, the Sun the afternoon. Final cards: For whoever asks the warm way and waits; The wind spent a minute, the sun spent the afternoon; Choose friction.

The North Wind first tried his power and blew with all his might, but the keener his blasts, the closer the Traveler wrapped his cloak around him, until at last, resigning all hope of victory, the Wind called upon the Sun to see what he could do. The Sun suddenly shone out with all his warmth. The Traveler no sooner felt his genial rays than he took off one garment after another, and at last, fairly overcome with heat, undressed and bathed in a stream that lay in his path.'
